events.title: IBM PC 5150 released
events.summary: [IBM] announced the Personal Computer model 5150 on August 12, 1981 — an open-architecture x86 machine that defined the [IBM] [PC] compatible standard.
events.about: The [IBM] [PC] used off-the-shelf parts (Intel 8088, [DOS] from [MS]) and published expansion specs — clones from Compaq and others followed. Developers wrote business software once and sold it to an entire industry. The "[PC]" in "[PC] programmer" means this machine and its descendants.

narrative.whyChosen: The [IBM] [PC] made the x86 + [DOS] platform the default for business and home computing worldwide.
narrative.whyImportant: Open expansion and clone compatibility created the largest software market in computing history.
narrative.problemSolved: Businesses wanted a trusted brand for desktops but needed a machine third parties could extend with cards and software.

events.title: MS-DOS 1.0 released with IBM PC
events.summary: [MS] shipped [MS-DOS] 1.0 on August 12, 1981 alongside the [IBM] [PC] — branded PC DOS by [IBM] but licensed to clone makers as [MS-DOS].
events.about: [DOS] gave the [IBM] [PC] a command-line file system, batch files, and a BIOS interface that clone manufacturers could license. The x86 + [DOS] stack became the default business platform for a decade — until Windows 95 finally hid the prompt for most users.

narrative.whyChosen: [MS-DOS] was the operating system layer that made [IBM] [PC] compatibles a unified software market.
narrative.whyImportant: One [OS] binary ran on [IBM]'s machine and every clone — the largest [PC] software ecosystem in history.
narrative.problemSolved: [PC] buyers needed disk management and a consistent program environment, not just bare metal.
